notes.h: Python fundamentals: types, control flow, functions
notes.body:
Python is dynamically typed: variables are names bound to objects, and the type belongs to the object, not the name. Everything is an object, and each has an identity, a type and a value.

Core types
- Immutable: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset. Mutable: list, dict, set.
- Integers have arbitrary precision. Floats are IEEE 754 doubles, so 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with math.isclose, not ==.
- // is floor division (−7 // 2 = −4) and % gives a remainder with the sign of the divisor (−7 % 3 = 2). ** is exponentiation.
- Strings are immutable sequences. Slicing s[start:stop:step] excludes stop, so s[::-1] reverses a string.

Control flow
- if / elif / else; for loops iterate over any iterable; while loops run until a condition fails; break and continue alter loops.
- Comprehensions build collections concisely: [x**2 for x in range(5) if x % 2 == 0] gives [0, 4, 16].
- Exceptions: try / except / else / finally. Catch specific exceptions (ValueError, KeyError) rather than a bare except.

Functions
- Defined with def; parameters can be positional, keyword, default, *args and **kwargs.
- Python passes object references ("call by sharing"). A function that mutates a list argument changes the caller's list, but rebinding the name inside the function does not.
- Scope follows LEGB: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in.
- Lambdas are small anonymous functions, often used as sort keys: sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]).

Aliasing and copying
b = a makes two names for the same list, so b.append(4) also changes a. Use a.copy() or list(a) for a shallow copy, and copy.deepcopy for nested structures.

Worked example: the mutable default trap
def add(x, lst=[]): lst.append(x); return lst
Calling add(1) and then add(2) returns [1, 2] the second time. The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and is shared between calls. The fix is lst=None, then if lst is None: lst = [] inside the body.

Good practice
- Follow PEP 8 naming (snake_case for functions and variables).
- Write docstrings, use type hints for readability, and keep functions small and testable.
- Use virtual environments to isolate package versions.

Exam pitfalls
- Confusing == (equal values) with is (same object).
- Using mutable default arguments.
- Off-by-one errors with range(n), which runs 0 to n − 1.
- Expecting floats to be exact.

Choosing the right data structure often matters more than clever code. Big-O notation describes how running time or memory grows with input size n in the worst case, ignoring constants.

Common complexities
- O(1) constant: dictionary lookup on average, list indexing.
- O(log n): binary search on a sorted list.
- O(n): a single pass, e.g. linear search or the in operator on a list.
- O(n log n): efficient comparison sorts such as merge sort, and Python's built-in Timsort.
- O(n²): nested loops over the same data, e.g. bubble sort or comparing all pairs.

Python's built-in structures
- list: dynamic array. Indexing O(1), append amortised O(1), insert or pop at the front O(n), membership O(n).
- tuple: immutable sequence; hashable if its contents are, so it can be a dict key.
- dict: hash table mapping keys to values. Average O(1) lookup, insert and delete. Keys must be hashable. Insertion order is preserved (guaranteed since Python 3.7).
- set: hash table of unique items. O(1) average membership; supports union, intersection and difference.
- collections.deque: O(1) appends and pops at both ends, ideal for queues. collections.Counter counts items; defaultdict supplies default values.
- Stacks are last in, first out (a list with append and pop); queues are first in, first out (a deque).

Key algorithms
- Linear search: check each item, O(n).
- Binary search: halve a sorted search range each step, O(log n). A million items need at most about 20 comparisons, since 2²⁰ ≈ 1.05 million.
- Merge sort: split, sort the halves recursively, merge. O(n log n) and stable.
- Recursion needs a base case and progress towards it. Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames, so deep recursion can fail.
- Memoisation caches results of repeated subproblems (functools.lru_cache). Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential; memoised, it becomes linear.

Worked example
To check which of 100,000 student IDs appear in a list of 50,000 enrolled IDs, testing membership in the list costs O(n·m), roughly 5 billion comparisons. Converting the enrolled list to a set first makes each check O(1) on average, so the whole job is roughly O(n + m).

Exam pitfalls
- Using a list for repeated membership tests where a set would do.
- Forgetting that binary search needs sorted input.
- Treating Big-O as exact timings; constants and real data sizes still matter.
- Using a mutable list as a dictionary key (TypeError: unhashable).

pandas is the standard Python library for tabular data. Its two core objects are the Series (a labelled one-dimensional array) and the DataFrame (a table of columns sharing an index). It is built on NumPy, so vectorised column operations are much faster than Python loops.

Loading and inspecting
- pd.read_csv, read_excel and read_parquet load data. Then df.head(), df.info() (types and non-null counts), df.describe() (summary statistics), df.shape and df.dtypes.

Selecting data
- Column: df["score"]. Several columns: df[["score", "hours"]].
- .loc selects by label and its slices include the end: df.loc[1:3] returns labels 1, 2 and 3.
- .iloc selects by integer position and excludes the end: df.iloc[1:3] returns positions 1 and 2.
- Boolean filtering: df.loc[df["hours"] > 9, "score"]. Combine conditions with & and |, with each condition in brackets.

Cleaning
- Missing values appear as NaN. Use df.isna().sum() to count them. Options are dropna(), fillna() (e.g. with the median), or an explicit model of missingness. Most aggregations, such as mean, skip NaN by default.
- Fix types with astype and pd.to_datetime; remove duplicates with drop_duplicates; clean text with the .str methods.

Transforming and combining
- New columns: df["rate"] = df["a"] / df["b"]. Use vectorised operations rather than apply where possible.
- Split–apply–combine: df.groupby("college")["score"].mean(), or .agg with several functions.
- merge joins tables on keys (inner, left, right, outer), like SQL joins. concat stacks frames.
- Reshape with pivot_table (long to wide) and melt (wide to long). Tidy data has one variable per column and one observation per row (Wickham, 2014).

Worked example
For a DataFrame with colleges UCL, LSE, UCL, KCL, LSE, UCL and scores 68, 72, NaN, 61, 65, 74, df.groupby("college")["score"].mean() gives KCL 61.0, LSE 68.5 and UCL 71.0, because the NaN is skipped. Note that .size() counts rows (UCL 3) while .count() counts non-missing values (UCL 2).

Exam pitfalls
- Chained indexing such as df[df.x > 0]["y"] = 1, which may modify a copy, not the original. Use df.loc[mask, "y"] = 1. (Since pandas 3.0, copy-on-write is the default, so chained assignment never changes the original frame and pandas issues a ChainedAssignmentError warning.)
- Using "and" or "or" instead of & or | in boolean masks.
- Merging on keys with duplicates and silently multiplying rows; check row counts after merges.
- Filling missing values with the mean before splitting into train and test sets, which leaks information.

Visualisation serves two purposes: exploration (finding patterns, outliers and errors for yourself) and communication (showing a clear message to others). Anscombe's quartet (1973) makes the case for plotting: four datasets with nearly identical means, variances, correlations and regression lines look completely different when graphed.

Choosing a chart
- Distribution of one variable: histogram (choose bin width carefully), density plot, box plot (median, quartiles, outliers).
- Relationship between two numeric variables: scatter plot; add a trend line or use transparency when points overlap.
- Change over time: line chart.
- Comparison across categories: bar chart, sorted where order is not meaningful. Bars must start at zero, because length encodes value.
- Part-to-whole: stacked bars, or a pie chart only for a few categories, since people judge angles poorly.
- Many variables: small multiples (facets), heatmaps, pair plots.

Perception and design
- Cleveland and McGill (1984) ranked visual encodings by how accurately people judge them. Position on a common scale is best, followed by position on non-aligned scales, then length, direction and angle, then area, with volume and colour shading weakest.
- Tufte's ideas: maximise the data-ink ratio and avoid "chartjunk" such as 3D effects and heavy gridlines.
- Use colour purposefully. Use sequential palettes for ordered data, diverging palettes for data around a meaningful midpoint, and categorical palettes for groups. Choose colour-blind-safe palettes (e.g. viridis) and never rely on colour alone.
- Always label axes with units, give a title that states the message, and cite the data source.

Python tools
- matplotlib: the foundation; fig, ax = plt.subplots() and then ax.plot, ax.scatter, ax.hist or ax.bar.
- seaborn: statistical plots built on matplotlib (histplot, boxplot, scatterplot with hue, pairplot).
- plotly or altair for interactive charts.

Worked example
Exam marks for two cohorts have similar means. A bar chart of means hides the fact that one cohort is bimodal. Overlaid histograms or side-by-side box plots reveal the different shapes, which matter for setting support.

Misleading practices to spot
- Truncated y-axes on bar charts that exaggerate small differences.
- Dual y-axes that suggest a relationship by choice of scale.
- Cherry-picked time windows, symbols scaled by radius instead of by area, and unequal bins presented without adjustment.

Exam pitfalls
- Choosing a chart for decoration instead of the question being asked.
- Over-plotting large datasets without transparency or binning.

notes.h: Probability and simulation for data science
notes.body:
Probability gives the language for uncertainty in data, models and predictions.

Core rules
- P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). Complement: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
- Conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B). Independence means P(A and B) = P(A)P(B).
- Bayes' theorem: P(H|D) = P(D|H)P(H)/P(D). This underlies naive Bayes classifiers and Bayesian updating.
- "At least one" problems are easiest via the complement: P(at least one six in 4 rolls) = 1 − (5/6)⁴ ≈ 0.518.

Random variables and distributions
- Expectation E[X] and variance Var(X) summarise a distribution. For a fair die, E[X] = 3.5 and Var(X) = 35/12 ≈ 2.92.
- Bernoulli and binomial for yes/no outcomes, Poisson for counts, uniform, normal for sums and averages, exponential for waiting times.
- The law of large numbers says averages settle down to the expected value; the central limit theorem says sample means are approximately normal in large samples.

Simulation (Monte Carlo)
When an analytic answer is hard, simulate. NumPy's generator API, rng = np.random.default_rng(seed), then rng.normal, rng.binomial or rng.choice, makes results reproducible. Monte Carlo error falls like 1/√(number of simulations).
- The bootstrap (Efron, 1979) resamples the data with replacement many times and recomputes a statistic each time. The spread of those values estimates the standard error or a confidence interval without strong distributional assumptions.
- Permutation tests shuffle group labels to build the null distribution of a difference.

A/B testing
Compare conversion rates between a control and a variant using a two-proportion z-test. For example, with 2000 users per arm and rates of 10% and 12%, the pooled rate is 11%. The SE is √(0.11 × 0.89 × (1/2000 + 1/2000)) ≈ 0.0099, giving z ≈ 2.02 and a two-sided p ≈ 0.043.

Worked example: the birthday problem
The probability that at least two of 23 people share a birthday is 1 − (365 × 364 × … × 343)/365²³ ≈ 0.507. This is easy to confirm by simulation and is a reminder that coincidences are commoner than intuition suggests.

Exam pitfalls
- The base-rate fallacy: confusing P(D|H) with P(H|D).
- Assuming independence when events are linked, e.g. repeated measurements on the same user.
- "Peeking" at an A/B test and stopping as soon as p < 0.05, which inflates false positives.
- Forgetting to set a seed, which makes results impossible to reproduce.

Regression predicts a numeric target y from features X. Unlike econometrics, where the focus is often a causal coefficient, prediction is judged by performance on new, unseen data.

Linear regression
- Model ŷ = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … + βₖxₖ, fitted by ordinary least squares (minimising the sum of squared residuals).
- Coefficients show associations holding other features fixed, not causal effects.
- In scikit-learn: model = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train), then model.predict(X_test).

Evaluation metrics
- MSE = mean of (y − ŷ)²; RMSE = √MSE is in the units of y and penalises large errors heavily.
- MAE = mean of |y − ŷ|; more robust to outliers.
- R² = 1 − SSres/SStot. On test data it can be negative if the model is worse than predicting the mean.

The bias–variance trade-off
Expected test error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Simple models underfit (high bias). Very flexible models, such as high-degree polynomials, overfit (high variance), with low training error but poor test error.

Controlling complexity
- Train/test split: hold out data that the model never sees during fitting.
- k-fold cross-validation: split the training data into k folds, train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining fold, rotating through all k. It is used to choose hyperparameters.
- Regularisation adds a penalty to OLS. Ridge (L2) adds λΣβⱼ², shrinking coefficients smoothly. Lasso (L1) adds λΣ|βⱼ| and can set some coefficients exactly to zero, performing variable selection (Tibshirani, 1996). Standardise features first so the penalty treats them equally.
- Feature engineering: polynomial terms, interactions, logs of skewed variables, one-hot encoding of categories.

Worked example
For hours studied x = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and scores y = 50, 58, 61, 70, 76: x̄ = 6, ȳ = 63, Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) = 128 and Σ(x − x̄)² = 40. So the slope is 3.2 and the intercept is 63 − 3.2 × 6 = 43.8. The prediction at 7 hours is 66.2, and the training R² is about 0.985. With five points, that R² says little about performance on new students.

Residual checks
Plot residuals against fitted values. Curvature suggests a missing nonlinearity; a funnel shape suggests heteroskedasticity.

Exam pitfalls
- Reporting training error as if it measured performance on new data.
- Tuning hyperparameters on the test set, which makes the test score optimistic.
- Fitting scalers or imputers on the full dataset before splitting (data leakage). Use a Pipeline.
- Reading predictive coefficients as causal.

notes.h: Classification and core machine learning methods
notes.body:
Classification predicts a categorical label, such as spam or not spam, from features. This is supervised learning, because training data include the correct labels. Unsupervised learning, such as k-means clustering or PCA, finds structure without labels.

Logistic regression
- Models P(y = 1|x) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)) with z = β₀ + β₁x₁ + … The sigmoid maps any z to a value between 0 and 1.
- Coefficients act on the log-odds: a one-unit rise in xⱼ multiplies the odds by e^βⱼ (e.g. β = 0.8 gives odds × 2.23).
- Fitted by maximum likelihood, minimising log loss (cross-entropy). Classify using a threshold, 0.5 by default, but tune it to the costs of errors.

k-nearest neighbours (kNN)
- Classify a point by majority vote among its k closest training points, usually by Euclidean distance.
- Small k gives a flexible, high-variance model; large k is smoother with more bias. Scale features first, or variables with large units dominate the distance.

Decision trees and ensembles
- Trees split the feature space with if–then rules chosen to reduce impurity. Gini impurity = 1 − Σpₖ²; entropy = −Σpₖ log₂ pₖ.
- Trees are easy to interpret but overfit unless pruned or depth-limited.
- Random forests (Breiman, 2001) average many trees grown on bootstrap samples, each considering random subsets of features at each split. This reduces variance.
- Gradient boosting builds trees sequentially, each correcting the previous ones' errors (e.g. XGBoost, LightGBM).

Other methods to recognise
- Naive Bayes applies Bayes' theorem, assuming features are conditionally independent given the class.
- Support vector machines find a maximum-margin boundary; kernels allow nonlinear boundaries.
- Neural networks stack layers of weighted sums and nonlinear activations, trained by gradient descent with backpropagation.

Worked example (Gini)
A node holds 4 positives and 6 negatives: Gini = 1 − (0.4² + 0.6²) = 0.48. A split sends 4 cases (3 positive) left and 6 cases (1 positive) right. The left Gini is 1 − (0.75² + 0.25²) = 0.375 and the right is 1 − ((1/6)² + (5/6)²) ≈ 0.278. The weighted impurity is 0.4 × 0.375 + 0.6 × 0.278 ≈ 0.317, so the split reduces impurity by about 0.163.

Exam pitfalls
- Calling logistic regression a regression method for continuous outcomes. It outputs probabilities used for classification.
- Forgetting to scale features for kNN and SVMs (trees do not need scaling).
- Treating a deep tree's perfect training accuracy as success.
- Feeding nominal categories as integer codes into a model such as linear or logistic regression or kNN, which then treats them as ordered numbers; one-hot encode them instead.

notes.h: Model evaluation, validation and responsible data science
notes.body:
Evaluation should reflect the real cost of mistakes and use unseen data.

The confusion matrix (binary classification)
- TP and TN are correct predictions; FP is a false alarm; FN is a miss.
- Accuracy = (TP + TN)/total. It is misleading when classes are imbalanced: predicting "no fraud" every time scores 99% if fraud is 1%.
- Precision = TP/(TP + FP): of the cases flagged, how many were right.
- Recall (sensitivity, true positive rate) = TP/(TP + FN): of the actual positives, how many were caught.
- Specificity = TN/(TN + FP). F1 = 2PR/(P + R).
- Lowering the threshold raises recall and usually lowers precision.

Threshold-free metrics
- The ROC curve plots TPR against FPR across thresholds. AUC is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative; 0.5 is chance.
- Precision–recall curves are more informative under heavy class imbalance.

Validation practice
- Keep a final test set untouched until the end. Use cross-validation on the training data for model selection; use stratified folds for imbalanced classes and time-based splits for time series.
- Data leakage means information from outside the training data, or from the future, entering the features. Examples include target-derived features and scaling before splitting.

Worked example
1000 loan applications, 100 of which default. The model flags 140: 80 true defaulters (TP) and 60 non-defaulters (FP), so FN = 20 and TN = 840. Accuracy = 0.92, precision = 80/140 ≈ 0.571, recall = 0.80, specificity = 840/900 ≈ 0.933 and F1 ≈ 0.667.

Ethics and fairness
- Bias can enter through unrepresentative data, historically biased labels, or proxies for protected characteristics (postcode can stand in for ethnicity).
- Fairness criteria include demographic parity (equal selection rates), equal opportunity (equal TPRs) and calibration within groups. When base rates differ, these cannot generally all hold at once (Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, 2016; Chouldechova, 2017).
- The COMPAS recidivism debate (ProPublica, 2016) showed different fairness metrics giving conflicting verdicts.
- UK law: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 require a lawful basis for processing, data minimisation and transparency, and they regulate solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (commenced in stages; its automated decision-making reforms in s.80 took effect on 5 February 2026) replaced Article 22 with Articles 22A–22D. Significant solely automated decisions are now generally permitted, with tighter limits where special category data are used, but controllers must provide safeguards: information about the decision and the ability to make representations, obtain human intervention and contest it. The Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination on protected characteristics.
- Good practice: document models (model cards), audit performance by subgroup, and keep humans in the loop for high-stakes decisions.

Exam pitfalls
- Reporting accuracy alone on imbalanced data.
- Assuming that removing a protected attribute makes a model fair (proxies remain).

cards.f: Name three mutable and three immutable built-in Python types.
cards.b: Mutable: list, dict, set. Immutable: int, str, tuple (also float, bool, frozenset).

cards.f: What does 7 // 2 return, and what does -7 // 2 return?
cards.b: 3 and −4. Floor division rounds down towards negative infinity, not towards zero.

cards.f: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 False in Python?
cards.b: Floats are stored in binary (IEEE 754), so 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented exactly; the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Use math.isclose.

cards.f: Difference between == and is?
cards.b: == tests whether values are equal; is tests whether two names refer to the same object.

cards.f: What is the mutable default argument pitfall?
cards.b: A default like lst=[] is created once when the function is defined and shared across calls, so changes persist. Use lst=None and create the list inside.

cards.f: After a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; b.append(4), what is a?
cards.b: [1, 2, 3, 4]. b is another name for the same list (aliasing); use a.copy() to get an independent list.

cards.f: Write a list comprehension for the squares of even numbers below 10.
cards.b: [x**2 for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0], which gives [0, 4, 16, 36, 64].

cards.f: What does s[::-1] do to a string s?
cards.b: Returns the string reversed, using a slice with step −1.

cards.f: What does the LEGB rule describe?
cards.b: The order Python searches for a name: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module), then Built-in.

cards.f: Purpose of *args and **kwargs?
cards.b: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict.

cards.f: Why catch specific exceptions rather than using a bare except?
cards.b: A bare except also hides unexpected errors (even KeyboardInterrupt), making bugs hard to find; catching e.g. ValueError handles only the anticipated problem.

cards.f: What does Big-O notation describe?
cards.b: How an algorithm's running time or memory grows with input size n, typically in the worst case, ignoring constant factors.

cards.f: Average time complexity of membership tests: list vs set?
cards.b: List: O(n), since it scans items. Set: O(1) on average, using a hash table.

cards.f: Time complexity of binary search, and its precondition?
cards.b: O(log n); the data must already be sorted.

cards.f: Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need for 1,000,000 items?
cards.b: About 20, since 2²⁰ ≈ 1.05 million.

cards.f: Why can't a list be a dictionary key?
cards.b: Dict keys must be hashable; lists are mutable, so their hash could change, and Python raises TypeError.

cards.f: Stack vs queue?
cards.b: A stack is last in, first out (e.g. list append/pop). A queue is first in, first out (e.g. collections.deque with append/popleft).

cards.f: Time complexity of merge sort?
cards.b: O(n log n) in all cases; it is also stable (equal items keep their order).

cards.f: Why is list.pop(0) slow and what should you use instead?
cards.b: Removing the first item shifts every other element, O(n). collections.deque.popleft() is O(1).

cards.f: What is memoisation?
cards.b: Caching results of function calls so repeated subproblems are not recomputed, e.g. with functools.lru_cache; naive recursive Fibonacci goes from exponential to linear time.

cards.f: Two essentials of a correct recursive function?
cards.b: A base case that stops recursion, and a recursive step that moves towards that base case.

cards.f: Complexity of comparing every pair in a list of n items?
cards.b: O(n²), since there are n(n − 1)/2 pairs.

cards.f: Series vs DataFrame?
cards.b: A Series is a labelled one-dimensional array; a DataFrame is a two-dimensional table of columns (Series) sharing one index.

cards.f: .loc vs .iloc?
cards.b: .loc selects by label and its slices include the end label; .iloc selects by integer position and excludes the end.

cards.f: How do you count missing values in each column?
cards.b: df.isna().sum().

cards.f: Why must you use & and | rather than and/or in pandas filters?
cards.b: and/or try to reduce a whole Series to one True/False and raise an error; & and | work element-wise. Wrap each condition in brackets.

cards.f: What does split–apply–combine mean?
cards.b: Split rows into groups (groupby), apply a function to each group (mean, sum, custom), and combine results into a new table.

cards.f: groupby .size() vs .count()?
cards.b: .size() counts all rows in each group; .count() counts non-missing values in each column.

cards.f: What is a left merge?
cards.b: Keeps every row of the left DataFrame and attaches matching rows from the right; unmatched rows get NaN.

cards.f: What risk comes with merging on non-unique keys?
cards.b: Duplicate keys on both sides produce every combination, silently multiplying rows; check shapes or use validate='one_to_one'.

cards.f: Define tidy data.
cards.b: Each variable is a column, each observation is a row, and each type of observational unit is a table (Wickham, 2014).

cards.f: What do pivot_table and melt do?
cards.b: pivot_table reshapes long data to wide with aggregation; melt reshapes wide data to long.

cards.f: Why prefer vectorised operations to apply or loops?
cards.b: Vectorised operations run in optimised compiled code on whole arrays and are typically much faster and clearer.

cards.f: What does Anscombe's quartet demonstrate?
cards.b: Four datasets with nearly identical summary statistics and regression lines look very different when plotted, so always visualise data.

cards.f: Best chart for the distribution of one numeric variable?
cards.b: A histogram or density plot; a box plot for comparing distributions across groups.

cards.f: Why must bar charts start at zero?
cards.b: Bars encode value by length, so a truncated axis exaggerates differences.

cards.f: Which visual encoding do people judge most accurately (Cleveland and McGill, 1984)?
cards.b: Position along a common scale, ahead of length, angle, area and colour shading.

cards.f: What is Tufte's data-ink ratio?
cards.b: The share of a graphic's ink that shows data; maximise it by removing non-essential decoration (chartjunk).

cards.f: When should you use a diverging colour palette?
cards.b: When values diverge from a meaningful midpoint, such as zero change or an average, e.g. profit/loss.

cards.f: How can you handle overplotting in a large scatter plot?
cards.b: Use transparency (alpha), smaller markers, hexbin or 2D density plots, or sampling.

cards.f: Why are pie charts often discouraged?
cards.b: People compare angles and areas less accurately than lengths; bar charts show the same comparison more clearly, especially with many categories.

cards.f: Create a figure and axes in matplotlib's object-oriented style.
cards.b: fig, ax = plt.subplots(), then call methods like ax.scatter(x, y) and ax.set_xlabel('...').

cards.f: Why can dual y-axis charts mislead?
cards.b: The two scales can be chosen to make any two series appear to move together, suggesting a relationship that may not exist.

cards.f: Exploratory vs explanatory visualisation?
cards.b: Exploratory charts help the analyst find patterns quickly; explanatory charts are polished to communicate one clear message to an audience.

cards.f: State Bayes' theorem.
cards.b: P(H|D) = P(D|H)P(H)/P(D): the posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.

cards.f: Probability of at least one six in four rolls of a fair die?
Expectation and variance of a fair six-sided die?
What does the law of large numbers say?
cards.b: As the number of independent trials grows, the sample average converges to the expected value.

cards.f: What is the bootstrap?
cards.b: Resampling the observed data with replacement many times and recomputing a statistic each time, to estimate its sampling variability (Efron, 1979).

cards.f: How does a permutation test work?
cards.b: Shuffle group labels repeatedly, recompute the test statistic each time to build its null distribution, and compare the observed value with it.

cards.f: Why set a random seed in a simulation?
cards.b: So results are reproducible; e.g. rng = np.random.default_rng(42).

cards.f: How does Monte Carlo error scale with the number of simulations N?
cards.b: It falls in proportion to 1/√N, so 100 times more simulations gives about 10 times more precision.

cards.f: What goes wrong if you 'peek' at an A/B test and stop when p < 0.05?
cards.b: Repeated looks inflate the false-positive rate well above 5%; use a fixed sample size or a sequential testing method.

cards.f: Which distribution suits the number of website visits per minute?
cards.b: The Poisson distribution, for counts of events in a fixed interval at a roughly constant rate.

cards.f: Define RMSE.
cards.b: Root mean squared error, √(mean of (y − ŷ)²); in the units of y and sensitive to large errors.

cards.f: MAE vs RMSE?
cards.b: MAE averages absolute errors and is more robust to outliers; RMSE squares errors so it penalises large misses more.

cards.f: Can test-set R² be negative?
cards.b: Yes, if the model predicts worse than simply using the mean of y.

cards.f: State the bias–variance decomposition of expected test error.
cards.b: Expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise.

cards.f: What is overfitting?
cards.b: A model fits noise in the training data, giving low training error but high error on new data.

cards.f: Describe k-fold cross-validation.
cards.b: Split the data into k folds; train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining fold, rotating so each fold validates once; average the scores.

cards.f: Ridge vs lasso regularisation?
cards.b: Ridge adds an L2 penalty λΣβ² that shrinks coefficients; lasso adds an L1 penalty λΣ|β| that can set some exactly to zero (variable selection).

cards.f: Why standardise features before ridge or lasso?
cards.b: The penalty depends on coefficient size, which depends on units; standardising makes the penalty treat features equally.

cards.f: What is data leakage in preprocessing?
cards.b: Fitting scalers, imputers or feature selection on the full dataset lets test information shape training; fit them on training data only, e.g. in a Pipeline.

cards.f: Effect of increasing λ in ridge regression?
cards.b: Coefficients shrink towards zero, raising bias and lowering variance; λ is chosen by cross-validation.

cards.f: Supervised vs unsupervised learning?
cards.b: Supervised learning uses labelled examples to predict a target; unsupervised learning finds structure such as clusters without labels.

cards.f: What function does logistic regression use to produce probabilities?
cards.b: The sigmoid, 1/(1 + e^(−z)), which maps any real z to a value between 0 and 1.

cards.f: Interpret a logistic coefficient of 0.8.
cards.b: A one-unit increase in the feature multiplies the odds of the positive class by e^0.8 ≈ 2.23, holding others fixed.

cards.f: Effect of small vs large k in kNN?
cards.b: Small k gives a flexible, noisy boundary (high variance); large k smooths it (higher bias).

cards.f: Why scale features for kNN?
cards.b: Distances are dominated by features with large numeric ranges unless all features are put on comparable scales.

cards.f: Gini impurity formula, and its value for a 50/50 node?
cards.b: Gini = 1 − Σpₖ²; for 50/50 it is 1 − (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.5, the maximum for two classes.

cards.f: How does a random forest reduce overfitting?
cards.b: It averages many trees trained on bootstrap samples, with random feature subsets at each split, lowering variance (Breiman, 2001).

cards.f: Bagging vs boosting?
cards.b: Bagging trains models independently on bootstrap samples and averages them; boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on the previous models' errors.

cards.f: Key assumption of naive Bayes?
cards.b: Features are conditionally independent given the class.

cards.f: What is k-means clustering?
cards.b: An unsupervised method that assigns points to k clusters by repeatedly assigning each point to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids.

cards.f: Do decision trees need feature scaling?
cards.b: No. Splits depend on orderings within each feature, so monotonic rescaling does not change the tree.

cards.f: Define precision and recall.
cards.b: Precision = TP/(TP + FP), the share of flagged cases that are positive. Recall = TP/(TP + FN), the share of actual positives caught.

cards.f: Why is accuracy misleading for imbalanced data?
cards.b: A model that always predicts the majority class can score highly (e.g. 99% when positives are 1%) while catching no positives.

cards.f: Define the F1 score.
cards.b: The harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR/(P + R).

cards.f: What does AUC represent?
cards.b: The probability that a randomly chosen positive is scored higher than a randomly chosen negative; 0.5 is chance, 1 is perfect.

cards.f: Effect of lowering a classifier's threshold?
cards.b: More cases are predicted positive, so recall rises and precision usually falls.

cards.f: Why use time-based splits for time series validation?
cards.b: Random splits let the model train on the future to predict the past, which leaks information and overstates performance.

cards.f: Define demographic parity and equal opportunity.
cards.b: Demographic parity: equal positive prediction rates across groups. Equal opportunity: equal true positive rates across groups.

cards.f: Why can't all fairness criteria usually hold at once?
cards.b: When base rates differ between groups, calibration and equal error rates are generally incompatible (Kleinberg et al., 2016; Chouldechova, 2017).

cards.f: Does dropping a protected attribute make a model fair?
cards.b: No. Other features such as postcode can act as proxies, so discrimination can persist.

cards.f: Which UK laws are most relevant to automated decisions on people?
cards.b: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025) for data and automated decisions, and the Equality Act 2010 for discrimination.

cards.f: What is a model card?
cards.b: Short documentation of a model's intended use, training data, performance (including by subgroup) and limitations.

questions.q: Which of these Python types is immutable?
questions.why: Tuples cannot be changed after creation; lists, dicts and sets can be modified in place.
