def add(x, lst=[]):
    lst.append(x)
    return lst
What does the second call, add(2), return after add(1) has already been called?
questions.why: The default list is created once at definition time and shared, so it still contains 1 when 2 is appended.

questions.q: What is the average time complexity of checking whether an item is in a Python set?
questions.why: Sets are hash tables, so membership tests take constant time on average.

questions.q: For a DataFrame with the default integer index 0–5, how many rows do df.loc[1:3] and df.iloc[1:3] return respectively?
questions.why: .loc slices by label and includes the end label (1, 2, 3); .iloc slices by position and excludes the end (1, 2).

questions.q: Which chart is best for showing how a single variable changes over time?
questions.why: Line charts use position along a time axis and show trends clearly.

questions.q: A bar chart comparing two banks' satisfaction scores (81% and 84%) uses a y-axis running from 80% to 85%. What is the main problem?
options: The truncated axis exaggerates a small difference because bar length encodes value
Percentages cannot be shown on bar charts
It should be a scatter plot
questions.why: With a baseline at 80%, the second bar looks four times as long as the first, though the gap is 3 points.

questions.q: A fair die is rolled four times. What is the probability of at least one six?
questions.why: Use the complement: the chance of no six in four rolls is (5/6)⁴, so subtract it from 1.

questions.q: A model has training RMSE 1.2 and test RMSE 9.8, while a simpler model has 4.1 and 4.5. The first model is most likely:
questions.why: A large gap between low training error and high test error is the signature of overfitting.

questions.q: In logistic regression, a coefficient of 0.8 on a feature means a one-unit increase in that feature:
options: Raises the probability by 80 percentage points
questions.why: Coefficients act on log-odds; e^0.8 ≈ 2.23 is the odds ratio. The effect on probability depends on the starting point.

questions.q: A cancer screening model has 95% accuracy on data where 5% of patients have cancer. What can you conclude?
options: Nothing about usefulness: always predicting 'no cancer' also gives 95% accuracy
Its recall must be at least 95%
Its precision must be at least 95%
questions.why: Under imbalance, accuracy can match a trivial classifier; check recall, precision and the confusion matrix.

questions.q: Explain the difference between b = a and b = a.copy() when a is a list, and when you would need copy.deepcopy.
markScheme: b = a creates an alias: both names refer to the same list, so changes via b show in a
a.copy() creates a new (shallow) list, so appending to b does not affect a
Shallow copies share nested objects; deepcopy is needed for nested mutable contents
questions.modelAnswer: b = a does not copy anything. It binds a second name to the same list, so b.append(4) also changes a. a.copy() builds a new outer list, so adding or removing items in b leaves a unchanged. The copy is shallow, though: if a contains inner lists, both copies share those inner objects. To copy a nested structure fully, use copy.deepcopy.

questions.q: Write a Python function has_pair(nums, target) that returns True if any two different numbers in nums sum to target, in O(n) average time. Explain why it is O(n).
markScheme: Uses a set of values seen so far
For each x checks whether target − x is in the set before adding x
Returns True on a match, else False after the loop
One pass with O(1) average set operations gives O(n), versus O(n²) for checking all pairs

questions.q: A DataFrame df has columns college, score (with missing values) and hours. Write pandas code to (a) count missing scores, (b) find the mean score by college, and (c) select scores of students who studied more than 9 hours.
markScheme: df['score'].isna().sum()
df.groupby('college')['score'].mean()
df.loc[df['hours'] > 9, 'score']
Notes that mean skips NaN by default
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) df['score'].isna().sum() counts missing scores.
(b) df.groupby('college')['score'].mean() returns the mean score for each college. By default pandas skips NaN when averaging, so each mean uses only the observed scores in that group.
(c) df.loc[df['hours'] > 9, 'score'] uses a boolean mask on the rows and selects the score column, avoiding chained indexing.

questions.q: A journalist wants to show (a) the distribution of London rents, (b) how rents relate to distance from the centre, (c) average rent by borough, and (d) the monthly trend in average rent. Recommend a chart for each, with a reason.
markScheme: (a) Histogram or box plot: shows shape, skew and outliers
(b) Scatter plot, perhaps with a trend line, for two numeric variables
(c) Sorted horizontal bar chart starting at zero for comparing categories
(d) Line chart for change over time
questions.modelAnswer: (a) A histogram, or a box plot, shows the shape of the rent distribution, including its right skew and expensive outliers. (b) A scatter plot of rent against distance shows the relationship; add a smoothed trend line and transparency if there are many points. (c) A horizontal bar chart sorted by value, starting at zero, makes borough comparisons easy and fits long names. (d) A line chart of monthly averages shows the trend and seasonality.

questions.q: In an A/B test with 2000 users per arm, the control converts at 10% and the variant at 12%. Using a pooled two-proportion z-test, find z and state your conclusion at the 5% level.
markScheme: Pooled p = 0.11
|z| > 1.96 (p ≈ 0.043), reject equal rates at 5%, but the evidence is modest
questions.modelAnswer: The pooled conversion rate is (200 + 240)/4000 = 0.11. The standard error is √(0.11 × 0.89 × (2/2000)) ≈ 0.0099. So z = (0.12 − 0.10)/0.0099 ≈ 2.02, with a two-sided p-value of about 0.043. Since this is below 0.05, we reject equal conversion rates. The variant appears better, but the result is close to the threshold, so it should only be trusted if the sample size was fixed in advance and nobody stopped the test early after peeking.

questions.q: What is the bootstrap and what is it used for?
markScheme: Resampling the data with replacement many times and recomputing the statistic
Used to estimate standard errors or confidence intervals without strong distributional assumptions
questions.modelAnswer: The bootstrap (Efron, 1979) treats the sample as a stand-in for the population. It draws many resamples of the same size with replacement and recomputes the statistic of interest, such as a median or a model coefficient, on each. The spread of these values estimates the statistic's standard error or gives a confidence interval, without needing a formula or normality.

questions.q: Explain k-fold cross-validation and why it is preferred to a single validation split for choosing a hyperparameter.
markScheme: Split training data into k folds
Train on k − 1 folds and validate on the held-out fold, rotating k times
Average the validation scores for each hyperparameter value
Uses all data for validation once, reducing the variance of the estimate; the test set stays untouched
questions.modelAnswer: In k-fold cross-validation the training data are split into k roughly equal folds, often 5 or 10. For each candidate hyperparameter, the model is trained k times, each time on k − 1 folds, and scored on the remaining fold. The k scores are averaged. Every observation is used for validation exactly once, so the estimate depends less on one lucky or unlucky split. The final test set is kept separate and used only once at the end.

questions.q: A node contains 10 positive and 10 negative cases. Split A sends 8 cases (7 positive) left and 12 cases (3 positive) right. Split B sends 10 cases (6 positive) left and 10 (4 positive) right. Using Gini impurity, which split is better?
markScheme: Parent Gini = 0.5
Split B: both children 0.48, weighted 0.48
Split A gives the bigger reduction (0.1875 vs 0.02), so choose A
questions.modelAnswer: The parent node is 50/50, so its Gini is 0.5. Split A: the left child is 7/8 positive, Gini = 1 − (0.875² + 0.125²) ≈ 0.219. The right child is 3/12 positive, Gini = 1 − (0.25² + 0.75²) = 0.375. The weighted Gini is 0.4 × 0.219 + 0.6 × 0.375 ≈ 0.3125. Split B: both children are 60/40, Gini = 0.48 each, weighted 0.48. Split A reduces impurity by about 0.19 against 0.02 for B, so A is chosen.

questions.q: A loan default model is applied to 1000 applicants, 100 of whom default. It flags 140, of whom 80 default. Compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
questions.modelAnswer: TP = 80 and FP = 140 − 80 = 60. FN = 100 − 80 = 20 and TN = 900 − 60 = 840. Accuracy = (80 + 840)/1000 = 0.92. Precision = 80/140 ≈ 0.571, so 57% of flagged applicants actually default. Recall = 80/100 = 0.80, so 80% of defaulters are caught. F1 = 2 × 0.571 × 0.8/(0.571 + 0.8) ≈ 0.667. The headline accuracy flatters the model because defaults are only 10% of cases.

questions.q: Explain why removing a protected characteristic such as ethnicity from a model's inputs does not guarantee the model is fair.
markScheme: Proxy variables (e.g. postcode, school, name) correlate with the protected characteristic
Historical bias in labels means the target itself may encode discrimination
Fairness must be checked by measuring outcomes and error rates by group, which may require the attribute for auditing
questions.modelAnswer: Other inputs often correlate with the protected characteristic. Postcode, school attended or first name can act as proxies, so the model can learn much the same pattern indirectly. If the training labels reflect past discrimination, for example who was historically approved, the model will reproduce it whatever the inputs. Fairness has to be assessed by outcomes: compare selection and error rates across groups. That auditing often requires the protected attribute to be collected and used carefully.

markScheme: (a) Returns 50.0
Off-by-one: range starts at 1 so marks[0] is skipped; sum 150 divided by 3
(b) Raises ZeroDivisionError because len(marks) is 0
(c) Filters out None, e.g. with a comprehension
Uses sum()/len() rather than manual indexing
Returns None (or raises a clear ValueError) when no valid marks
Includes a docstring / type hints
(d) Test normal case [60, 70, 80] → 70.0
Test edge cases: list with None values, empty list or all None
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) It returns 50.0. range(1, len(marks)) produces indices 1 and 2, so marks[0] = 60 is never added. The total is 70 + 80 = 150, but it is divided by all 3 items, giving 50.0 instead of the correct 70.0. This is a classic off-by-one error. Iterating directly over the list with for m in marks avoids indices altogether.

(b) With an empty list the loop does not run, total stays 0, and 0/0 raises ZeroDivisionError.

(c) An idiomatic version:

def mean_marks(marks: list) -> float | None:
    """Return the mean of the non-missing marks, or None if there are none."""
    valid = [m for m in marks if m is not None]
    if not valid:
        return None
    return sum(valid) / len(valid)

The list comprehension drops None values, and the denominator counts only valid marks, so absent students do not drag the average down. The built-ins sum and len replace manual indexing. The empty case is handled explicitly. Returning None is one reasonable choice; raising ValueError('no valid marks') is another, and the docstring should say which behaviour callers can expect. statistics.mean could also be used after filtering.

(d) Tests (e.g. with pytest):
- assert mean_marks([60, 70, 80]) == 70.0 for the normal case, which would have caught the original bug.
- assert mean_marks([60, None, 80]) == 70.0 to check that missing values are ignored.
- assert mean_marks([]) is None and mean_marks([None]) is None for the edge cases.
These show the value of testing ordinary inputs and boundary cases separately.

questions.q:
A university's IT team stores 2 million student records as a Python list of (student_id, name) tuples. Every day it receives 50,000 IDs from a library system and must find each student's name. The current code loops over the full list for every incoming ID.
(a) State the time complexity of the current approach and estimate the number of comparisons. (3 marks)
(b) Propose two better approaches, giving their complexities and trade-offs. (7 marks)
(c) Explain how binary search works and how many steps it needs here. (5 marks)
markScheme: Worst case about 10¹¹ comparisons (on average about half that for found IDs)
Approach 1: build a dict {id: name} once in O(n), then each lookup O(1) average, total O(n + m)
Dict trade-off: extra memory; requires hashable, unique keys
Approach 2: sort by ID once O(n log n), then binary search each query O(log n), total O(n log n + m log n)
Sorting trade-off: slower lookups than a dict but supports range queries / lower memory
Mentions a database index or pandas merge as a practical alternative
Binary search: compare with the middle, discard half, repeat until found or empty
Needs about log₂(2,000,000) ≈ 21 comparisons per lookup
Requires sorted data
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Each of the m = 50,000 queries scans up to n = 2,000,000 records, so the cost is O(n·m). In the worst case that is 10¹¹ comparisons; IDs that are found need about half that on average. Either way, it is far too slow for a daily job in pure Python.

(b) Approach 1, hash table: build lookup = dict(records) once, which is O(n). Each query is then lookup.get(sid), O(1) on average, so the total is O(n + m), a few million operations. The trade-offs are extra memory for the dict and the need for unique, hashable keys, which IDs are. This is the natural choice for exact-match lookups.

Approach 2, sort and binary search: sort the records by ID once, O(n log n), then binary search for each query, O(log n) each. The total is O(n log n + m log n). Lookups are slower than with a dict, but a sorted array uses less memory and also supports range queries, such as all IDs between two values. The bisect module implements this.

In practice, the records probably belong in a database with an index on student_id. Alternatively, both datasets could be loaded into pandas and joined with a single merge, which uses hashing internally.

(c) Binary search keeps a range [lo, hi] over a sorted list. Each step compares the target with the middle element. If they are equal, the search ends. If the target is larger, the search continues in the upper half; if smaller, in the lower half. The range halves each time, so at most about ⌈log₂ n⌉ comparisons are needed. For n = 2,000,000 that is 21, since 2²¹ ≈ 2.1 million. It only works on data sorted by the search key, and boundary updates (lo = mid + 1, hi = mid − 1) are a common source of bugs.

questions.q:
Hannah, an analyst at a student housing company, has two CSV files: bookings.csv (booking_id, student_id, property_id, start_date, monthly_rent) and properties.csv (property_id, borough, bedrooms). Some rents are missing, some property IDs in bookings are absent from properties.csv, and start_date is stored as text.
Describe, with pandas code, how she would clean and combine the data to report median monthly rent by borough and year, and explain the checks she should make at each stage.
markScheme: Loads with pd.read_csv and inspects with info/head/describe/isna().sum()
Converts start_date with pd.to_datetime (errors='coerce') and checks failures
Investigates missing rents rather than blindly filling; median robust to outliers
Checks duplicates (drop_duplicates on booking_id) and invalid values (negative/zero rents)
Merges with how='left' on property_id and validate='many_to_one'
Checks row count unchanged after merge and counts unmatched properties (indicator=True)
Extracts year with .dt.year
groupby(['borough', 'year'])['monthly_rent'].median() (and count for sample sizes)
Reports group sizes and notes small groups
Documents decisions / reproducible script
questions.modelAnswer:
Load and inspect:
b = pd.read_csv('bookings.csv'); p = pd.read_csv('properties.csv')
b.info(); b.describe(); b.isna().sum()
This shows column types, missing counts and implausible values, such as zero or negative rents.

Clean the bookings:
- Dates: b['start_date'] = pd.to_datetime(b['start_date'], errors='coerce'). Then check b['start_date'].isna().sum() to find strings that failed to parse instead of letting them disappear silently.
- Duplicates: b = b.drop_duplicates('booking_id'), after checking whether duplicates are true repeats or data errors.
- Rents: investigate missing values first. Are they cancelled bookings or a particular property? For a median-rent report, the simplest defensible choice is to exclude missing rents from the calculation, which pandas does by default, and report how many were excluded. Imputing with an overall median would pull groups towards the average. Flag or remove impossible values with a boolean mask, e.g. b.loc[b['monthly_rent'] <= 0, 'monthly_rent'] = np.nan.

Combine:
m = b.merge(p, on='property_id', how='left', validate='many_to_one', indicator=True)
A left join keeps every booking. validate raises an error if property IDs are duplicated in properties.csv, which would otherwise multiply rows. Then assert len(m) == len(b) and check (m['_merge'] == 'left_only').sum() to count bookings with unknown properties. Report these rather than dropping them silently, or chase the missing property records.

Aggregate:
m['year'] = m['start_date'].dt.year
out = m.groupby(['borough', 'year'])['monthly_rent'].agg(['median', 'count']).reset_index()
The median is robust to a few luxury flats. The count column shows how many bookings support each figure, so readers can discount small groups. A pivot_table with boroughs as rows and years as columns makes a readable report.

Throughout, Hannah should keep this as a reproducible script, not manual edits, and record each cleaning decision.

questions.q:
Ravi produces a slide for the board of a coffee chain. It is a 3D pie chart of revenue share across 9 product lines, using a rainbow palette, alongside a bar chart of store satisfaction (scores 7.1 to 7.6) whose y-axis starts at 7.0. A second chart overlays monthly revenue and staff numbers on two different y-axes and is titled 'Hiring drives revenue'.
Critique these charts and propose improved designs.
markScheme: 3D distorts angles/areas; front slices look larger
Pie with 9 categories hard to compare; angles judged poorly (Cleveland and McGill, 1984)
Replace with a sorted horizontal bar chart, possibly grouping small categories
Rainbow palette not colour-blind safe, implies false order; use a single colour plus highlight
Truncated bar axis exaggerates small differences; bars must start at zero
Alternative: dot plot with a narrower axis is acceptable since position not length encodes value
Dual axes: scale choice can manufacture apparent co-movement
Causal title not supported by correlation; use neutral, descriptive title
Better: indexed lines on a common scale or two aligned panels
General: clear labels, units, source, a message-led but honest title
questions.modelAnswer:
The pie chart has three problems. The 3D effect distorts angles and areas, so front slices look bigger than they are. With nine categories, people must compare angles, which Cleveland and McGill (1984) found we judge far less accurately than positions or lengths. The rainbow palette adds no information, suggests an order that does not exist, and is hard for colour-blind viewers. A better design is a horizontal bar chart sorted by revenue share, in one neutral colour, with the product line under discussion highlighted. Very small lines could be grouped into 'Other'. Direct labels with percentages remove the need for a legend.

The satisfaction chart truncates the axis at 7.0, so a store scoring 7.6 has a bar six times as long as one scoring 7.1. That is a gross exaggeration, because bar length is read as magnitude. Either start the bars at zero, accepting that the differences look small because they are small, or switch to a dot plot. A dot plot encodes value by position, not length, so a narrower axis range is acceptable if it is clearly labelled. Adding confidence intervals would show whether the differences are meaningful at all.

The dual-axis chart is the most misleading. By choosing the two scales, almost any pair of upward-trending series can be made to overlap, suggesting a tight relationship. The title then claims causation, but staff and revenue may both be rising with seasonal demand or new store openings, and hiring may respond to revenue rather than drive it. Better options are to plot both series as an index (e.g. January = 100) on one axis, or to show two vertically aligned panels sharing the time axis. The title should be descriptive: 'Revenue and staff numbers both rose through 2026'.

Across all charts: label axes with units, cite the data source, remove chartjunk, and make sure the title states a message the data actually support.

questions.q:
A data science society wants to explain the birthday problem: in a group of 30 people, how likely is it that at least two share a birthday?
(a) Derive the exact probability, assuming 365 equally likely birthdays. (5 marks)
(b) Outline NumPy code for a Monte Carlo simulation of 10,000 groups, and explain how to judge its accuracy. (6 marks)
(c) Discuss which assumptions are unrealistic and how the simulation could relax them. (4 marks)
markScheme: Uses complement: P(all different) = 365 × 364 × … × 336/365³⁰
P(at least one match) ≈ 0.706
Explains intuition: 435 pairs of people
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) for reproducibility
Draws integers 0–364 of shape (10000, 30)
Checks each row for duplicates (e.g. comparing len(np.unique(row)) to 30) and averages
Monte Carlo SE = √(p(1 − p)/N) ≈ 0.0046
Estimate should be within about ±0.009 of 0.706 (95%)
Real birthdays are not uniform (seasonal patterns) and leap days exist
Simulation can sample from empirical birth frequencies; non-uniformity raises the match probability
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) It is easiest to compute the complement, that all 30 birthdays differ. The first person can have any birthday, the second must avoid one day (364/365), the third two days (363/365), and so on. P(all different) = (365 × 364 × … × 336)/365³⁰ ≈ 0.294. So P(at least one shared birthday) ≈ 1 − 0.294 = 0.706. The result surprises people because they think about matching their own birthday, whereas there are 30 × 29/2 = 435 pairs, each with a small chance of matching.

(b) Outline:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
b = rng.integers(0, 365, size=(10_000, 30))
shared = np.array([len(np.unique(row)) < 30 for row in b])
estimate = shared.mean()

Each row is one simulated group. A group has a shared birthday if it has fewer than 30 unique values, and the proportion of such rows estimates the probability. A faster vectorised method sorts each row and checks for equal neighbours: (np.diff(np.sort(b, axis=1), axis=1) == 0).any(axis=1). Setting the seed makes the result reproducible.

Accuracy: each group is a Bernoulli trial, so the Monte Carlo standard error is √(p(1 − p)/N) = √(0.706 × 0.294/10,000) ≈ 0.0046. A 95% interval is about ±0.009, so an estimate between roughly 0.697 and 0.715 is consistent with the exact answer. Quadrupling N would halve the error.

(c) The model assumes birthdays are independent and uniform over 365 days. In reality there are seasonal patterns, fewer births on weekends and holidays in countries with scheduled deliveries, and leap-day birthdays. Twins in a group would break independence. Non-uniform birthdays actually raise the chance of a match. A simulation can relax these assumptions easily by drawing from empirical daily birth frequencies (rng.choice with a p= vector over 366 days), which is a key advantage of simulation over closed-form algebra.

questions.q:
PropertyPulse, a London estate agency, builds a model to predict flat sale prices from 40 features using 3,000 past sales. Their analyst Zara fits a degree-5 polynomial regression with all interactions and reports R² = 0.97. She first standardised and imputed all features on the full dataset, then split 80/20 into train and test sets, then tried 30 model variants and kept the one with the best test score.
Evaluate Zara's approach and set out a sounder modelling workflow.
markScheme: Degree-5 polynomial with all interactions creates huge numbers of features relative to 3,000 rows: overfitting / high variance
Unclear whether R² = 0.97 is training or test; training R² is not evidence of predictive performance
Preprocessing on full data before split is leakage
Selecting among 30 variants by test score makes the test score optimistically biased
Proposes train/validation/test or cross-validation on training data for model selection
Use a Pipeline so imputation and scaling are fitted within each fold
Regularisation (ridge/lasso) or simpler models; tune λ by CV
Consider log price target given skew; report RMSE/MAE in £ as well as R²
Check residuals and performance by segment (e.g. borough, price band)
Time-aware split if predicting future sales (market changes)
questions.modelAnswer:
Zara's approach has several serious flaws, each of which makes the reported performance look better than it will be in use.

Model complexity. A degree-5 polynomial expansion of 40 features with all interactions produces an enormous number of terms, far more than the 3,000 observations. Such a model can fit almost any training data, so a high R² mainly reflects memorisation (high variance). If 0.97 is the training R², it says nothing about predictive ability.

Leakage in preprocessing. Standardising and imputing on the full dataset before splitting means the test data influenced the means, standard deviations and imputed values used in training. The test set is no longer truly unseen.

Test-set reuse. Trying 30 variants and keeping the one with the best test score turns the test set into a validation set. The winning score is biased upwards by selection: with enough tries, one variant will do well by chance.

A sounder workflow:
- Split off a test set first, using a time-based split if the model will predict future sales, since prices drift. Do not touch it until the end.
- Put preprocessing in a scikit-learn Pipeline (SimpleImputer, StandardScaler, then the model), so it is refitted within each training fold.
- Use k-fold cross-validation on the training data to compare candidates: a linear baseline, ridge or lasso with λ tuned by CV, and tree ensembles such as random forests or gradient boosting, which capture nonlinearities without manual polynomial expansion.
- Prices are right-skewed, so model log price and back-transform carefully.
- Report RMSE or MAE in pounds as well as R², because the business cares about the size of errors.
- Evaluate the chosen model once on the test set. Inspect residuals and performance by borough and price band to find segments where it fails.

Finally, document the process, and remember that coefficients from a predictive model describe associations, not the causal value of features.

questions.q:
FinFirst Bank fits a logistic regression to predict loan default: z = −2.0 + 0.03 × (credit utilisation, %) + 0.6 × (number of late payments in the past year), with P(default) = 1/(1 + e^(−z)).
(a) Calculate the predicted default probability for Ali (utilisation 40%, 1 late payment) and Beth (utilisation 80%, 2 late payments). (5 marks)
(b) Interpret the coefficient on late payments as an odds ratio. (3 marks)
(c) The bank declines applicants with P(default) above 0.5. Discuss how it should choose this threshold. (4 marks)
markScheme: Ali approved and Beth declined at 0.5
Odds ratio e^0.6 ≈ 1.82: each late payment multiplies odds by about 1.82, holding utilisation fixed
Effect on probability depends on baseline (non-linear)
Threshold should reflect costs of false negatives (defaults) vs false positives (lost good customers)
Use validation data: precision–recall / ROC trade-offs, expected profit; check calibration and fairness by group
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Ali: z = −2.0 + 0.03 × 40 + 0.6 × 1 = −2.0 + 1.2 + 0.6 = −0.2. P = 1/(1 + e^0.2) ≈ 1/(1 + 1.221) ≈ 0.45.
Beth: z = −2.0 + 0.03 × 80 + 0.6 × 2 = −2.0 + 2.4 + 1.2 = 1.6. P = 1/(1 + e^(−1.6)) ≈ 1/(1 + 0.202) ≈ 0.83.
At a 0.5 threshold, Ali is approved, narrowly, and Beth is declined.

(b) The coefficient 0.6 acts on the log-odds. Each additional late payment multiplies the odds of default by e^0.6 ≈ 1.82, an 82% increase in the odds, holding utilisation constant. This is not an 82% or 0.6-point increase in probability. Because the sigmoid is nonlinear, the change in probability depends on the starting point: it is largest for applicants near 0.5 and small for those with very low or very high risk.

(c) The 0.5 threshold implicitly treats a missed defaulter and a wrongly rejected good customer as equally costly, which is rarely true. A default might lose much of the loan, while rejecting a good applicant loses only the interest margin. The bank should estimate these costs and pick the threshold that maximises expected profit, or that meets a target default rate, using a validation set not used for fitting. Precision–recall or ROC curves show the trade-off. It should also check that predicted probabilities are calibrated. Because lending decisions are high-stakes, it should test whether error rates differ across protected groups, consistent with the Equality Act 2010, and give applicants meaningful explanations and a route to human review.

questions.q: 'Complex machine learning models such as random forests and neural networks should always be preferred to simple models such as logistic regression, because they are more accurate.' Discuss.
markScheme: Flexible models can capture nonlinearities and interactions and often win on large, complex data (images, text)
No free lunch: no method is best for every problem
On small or tabular datasets simple models often perform comparably; ensembles may win modestly
Bias–variance: complex models need more data and risk overfitting without regularisation and tuning
Accuracy is not the only criterion: interpretability, explainability for regulated decisions
Calibration, robustness to distribution shift, stability
Cost, latency, maintenance, reproducibility
Legal/ethical: UK GDPR automated decision safeguards, Equality Act; need to explain and audit
Good practice: start with a simple baseline, compare with cross-validation, use explanation tools (feature importance, SHAP) with caution
Balanced conclusion: choice depends on data, stakes and purpose
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim has some basis but goes too far. Flexible models such as random forests (Breiman, 2001), gradient boosting and neural networks can represent nonlinearities and high-order interactions automatically. On large, rich datasets such as images, audio, text or millions of transactions, they often clearly outperform linear models. Gradient-boosted trees are frequently among the strongest performers on tabular prediction tasks.

But 'always' fails for several reasons.

The 'no free lunch' idea says that no single method is best on every problem. With small samples, noisy outcomes or mostly linear relationships, a regularised logistic regression often matches complex models within sampling error. Flexible models have high variance: they need more data, careful tuning and cross-validation to avoid overfitting, and a poorly tuned forest can lose to a simple baseline.

Accuracy is also not the only objective.
- Interpretability. Logistic coefficients map directly to odds ratios that domain experts can check against common sense. Post-hoc explanation tools such as feature importance or SHAP values help with black-box models, but they approximate and can mislead.
- Accountability. In lending, hiring or healthcare, organisations must be able to justify decisions. UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 give people safeguards over significant solely automated decisions, including the right to contest them. The Equality Act 2010 requires organisations to avoid discriminatory outcomes. Opaque models make auditing harder.
- Robustness and calibration. Complex models can latch onto spurious patterns that fail under distribution shift, and their probability estimates are not always well calibrated.
- Practical costs. Training time, latency, monitoring and maintenance all grow with complexity.

Good practice is to start with a simple, well-understood baseline. Compare candidates on held-out data with metrics that reflect real costs, and adopt a complex model only if its gains are meaningful and its risks manageable. For high-stakes decisions, a slightly less accurate but transparent model may be the responsible choice. In conclusion, model choice depends on the data, the stakes and the purpose, not on complexity for its own sake.

questions.q:
HireSmart sells a CV-screening model to UK employers. On validation data it reports 80% accuracy. Broken down by applicant group:
Group A: 200 applicants, 100 qualified; the model shortlists 120, of whom 90 are qualified.
Group B: 100 applicants, 60 qualified; the model shortlists 40, of whom 36 are qualified.
(a) Compute the selection rate, true positive rate and precision for each group. (6 marks)
(b) Assess the model against demographic parity and equal opportunity. (4 marks)
(c) Discuss the possible causes, the legal and ethical issues, and what HireSmart should do. (6 marks)
markScheme: Group A: selection rate 120/200 = 0.60
Group A: TPR 90/100 = 0.90, precision 90/120 = 0.75
Group B: selection rate 40/100 = 0.40
Group B: TPR 36/60 = 0.60, precision 36/40 = 0.90
Demographic parity violated (0.60 vs 0.40; ratio ≈ 0.67)
Equal opportunity violated: qualified B applicants much less likely to be shortlisted (0.60 vs 0.90)
Higher precision for B shows the model is stricter on B: applies a higher bar
Causes: biased historical labels, proxies, unrepresentative training data
Legal: Equality Act 2010 (indirect discrimination), UK GDPR/DPA 2018 automated decision safeguards and transparency
Actions: audit features for proxies, retrain/reweight, adjust thresholds, human review, documentation and ongoing monitoring
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Group A: selection rate = 120/200 = 0.60. TPR = 90/100 = 0.90. Precision = 90/120 = 0.75.
Group B: selection rate = 40/100 = 0.40. TPR = 36/60 = 0.60. Precision = 36/40 = 0.90.
(Overall accuracy is 160/200 = 0.80 for A and 72/100 = 0.72 for B, so the headline 80% is not uniform.)

(b) Demographic parity requires equal selection rates. Here they are 0.60 against 0.40, a ratio of about 0.67, so parity fails. Base rates also differ (50% against 60% qualified), so parity is not necessarily the right benchmark. Equal opportunity is more telling. A qualified applicant from group B has only a 60% chance of being shortlisted, against 90% in group A, even though group B has the higher share of qualified applicants. Group B's higher precision confirms that the model applies a stricter bar to that group: it shortlists them only when very confident.

(c) Likely causes:
- training labels drawn from past hiring decisions that disadvantaged group B
- proxy features such as university, postcode, employment gaps or wording in CVs
- fewer group B examples in the training data, giving noisier scores.

Legally, systematically disadvantaging applicants who share a protected characteristic can amount to indirect discrimination under the Equality Act 2010 unless it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. Employers using the tool remain liable. Under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, significant solely automated decisions need safeguards such as transparency, the ability to contest and human intervention. A data protection impact assessment would be expected. Ethically, the tool risks entrenching exclusion at scale.

HireSmart should audit features for proxies and remove or constrain them. It should retrain with reweighting or fairness constraints, or calibrate thresholds by group within legal limits, and validate on representative data. It should publish subgroup metrics in a model card, require human review of rejections, and monitor outcomes after deployment.

questions.q:
A hospital trust develops a model to flag patients at risk of sepsis from vital signs. Of 2,000 test patients, 100 develop sepsis. At threshold 0.5 the model flags 150 patients, 70 of whom develop sepsis. Lowering the threshold to 0.3 flags 300 patients, 90 of whom develop sepsis.
(a) Compute recall, precision and specificity at each threshold. (6 marks)
(b) Recommend a threshold, justifying your choice. (4 marks)
(c) Identify two risks in evaluating this model and how to address them. (2 marks)
markScheme: Threshold 0.5: TP 70, FP 80, FN 30, TN 1820
Recall 0.70, precision ≈ 0.467, specificity 1820/1900 ≈ 0.958
Threshold 0.3: TP 90, FP 210, FN 10, TN 1690
Recall 0.90, precision 0.30, specificity 1690/1900 ≈ 0.889
Recognises missed sepsis (FN) is very costly; favours higher recall
Weighs alert fatigue from more false positives (workload)
Justified recommendation (e.g. 0.3 with clinical review) referring to costs
Risk: leakage (features recorded after diagnosis) or non-representative test data; address via temporal/external validation and subgroup checks
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Threshold 0.5: TP = 70, FP = 150 − 70 = 80, FN = 100 − 70 = 30, TN = 1900 − 80 = 1820.
Recall = 70/100 = 0.70. Precision = 70/150 ≈ 0.467. Specificity = 1820/1900 ≈ 0.958.

Threshold 0.3: TP = 90, FP = 300 − 90 = 210, FN = 10, TN = 1900 − 210 = 1690.
Recall = 90/100 = 0.90. Precision = 90/300 = 0.30. Specificity = 1690/1900 ≈ 0.889.

(b) The costs of the two errors are very unequal. A missed case of sepsis can be fatal, while a false alarm mainly costs clinician time and possibly extra tests. Lowering the threshold to 0.3 cuts missed cases from 30 to 10, a large gain in recall. The cost is 130 extra false alarms, and precision falls from about 47% to 30%, so roughly one flag in three is a true case. That is likely to be acceptable if a flag triggers a quick clinical review rather than automatic treatment. The main risk of the lower threshold is alert fatigue: if staff learn that most alerts are false, they may start ignoring them. I would recommend 0.3, or a tiered system with urgent alerts above 0.5 and lower-priority review between 0.3 and 0.5. The choice should be made with clinicians and monitored after deployment.

(c) First, leakage. Features recorded after clinicians already suspected sepsis, such as antibiotic orders or blood culture requests, would inflate performance; use only data available at prediction time. Second, generalisability. Validate on later time periods and other hospitals, and check performance across subgroups such as age and ethnicity, because vital-sign patterns and data recording practices differ.

markScheme: Recurrence: the last move is either 1 step (ways(n − 1)) or 2 steps (ways(n − 2)); base cases ways(1) = 1, ways(2) = 2
Call tree branches twice per call; subproblems recomputed many times
Running time grows exponentially, roughly like the Fibonacci numbers (about 1.618ⁿ)
ways(30) makes over 1.6 million calls (1,664,079)
Memoised version with functools.lru_cache: O(n) time, O(n) space
Iterative bottom-up version keeping two variables: O(n) time, O(1) space
Correct code for at least one improved version
Recursion depth: memoised recursive version needs about n nested frames; default limit about 1000 raises RecursionError
Iterative version has no recursion depth problem; Python ints have arbitrary precision so large results are fine

questions.q:
An admissions officer at Harcourt College uses pandas to analyse applications to two courses:
Course X: 100 male applicants (80 admitted), 20 female applicants (18 admitted).
Course Y: 20 male applicants (4 admitted), 100 female applicants (30 admitted).
She runs df.groupby('sex')[['applied', 'admitted']].sum() and concludes the college discriminates against women.
(a) Compute the overall and course-level admission rates by sex. (6 marks)
(b) Explain the apparent contradiction. (6 marks)
(c) Show how to produce the course-level comparison in pandas, and explain why averaging the course rates is not a full fix. (4 marks)
(d) What would you need to know before drawing conclusions about discrimination? (4 marks)
markScheme: Course X: men 0.80, women 0.90
Course Y: men 0.20, women 0.30
Women have higher rates in each course despite lower overall rate: Simpson's paradox
Explains confounding: women apply mainly to the more selective course Y
Links to Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (1975) Berkeley admissions study
pandas: compute rate column then pivot_table(index='course', columns='sex', values='rate') or groupby(['course', 'sex'])
Unweighted mean of course rates ignores differing applicant numbers; better to standardise or model with course as a control (e.g. logistic regression)
Need applicant qualifications / grades; the direction of causation in course choice
Consider whether course selectivity itself reflects structural issues; aggregation level matters
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Overall, men applied 120 times with 84 admitted, a rate of 0.70. Women also applied 120 times with 48 admitted, a rate of 0.40. By course: in X, men 80/100 = 0.80 and women 18/20 = 0.90; in Y, men 4/20 = 0.20 and women 30/100 = 0.30. Women have the higher admission rate in both courses but a much lower rate overall.

(b) This is Simpson's paradox: an association in aggregated data reverses within every subgroup. The cause is a confounder, course choice, linked to both sex and the outcome. Most women applied to course Y, which admits few applicants of either sex. Most men applied to course X, which admits most applicants. The overall rates therefore mostly reflect which course people applied to, not how each sex was treated within a course. The classic real example is the University of California, Berkeley graduate admissions analysis by Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell (1975), where an apparent bias against women largely disappeared within departments.

(c) In pandas:
df['rate'] = df['admitted'] / df['applied']
df.pivot_table(index='course', columns='sex', values='rate')
or df.groupby(['course', 'sex'])[['applied', 'admitted']].sum() before dividing. Simply averaging the course-level rates by sex (women 0.60, men 0.50 here) gives each course equal weight however many people applied. That can mislead in other datasets. Better approaches are direct standardisation, which applies each sex's course-specific rates to a common applicant mix, or a logistic regression of admission on sex with course fixed effects, which estimates the within-course difference.

(d) Before concluding anything about discrimination, we would need applicants' qualifications such as grades and interview scores, since rates conditional on course may still differ in merit. We would also want to know why women apply disproportionately to course Y. If the selectivity of courses popular with women reflects under-funding, the disadvantage is structural even if each admissions decision is fair. The right level of aggregation depends on the causal question being asked.

questions.q: 'If a machine learning model predicts an outcome accurately, its most important features tell us what we should change to improve that outcome.' Discuss, with reference to regression and prediction.
markScheme: Distinguishes prediction (estimating E[y|x] for new cases) from causal inference (effect of intervening on x)
Predictive features can be correlated with the outcome through confounding or reverse causality
Example: hospital or education setting where a predictor is a marker, not a cause
Regularisation (lasso) picks among correlated features somewhat arbitrarily; importance unstable
Coefficients/importances depend on which other variables are included (omitted variable bias)
Feature importance measures (permutation, SHAP) explain the model, not the world
Intervening changes the data distribution; model learned under observational conditions (distribution shift / Goodhart's law)
Causal methods needed: randomised experiments, A/B tests, natural experiments, IV, DiD
Prediction still useful: targeting resources, forecasting, risk scoring
Balanced conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement mixes up two different tasks. A predictive model estimates E[y | x] well for new cases drawn from the same population. A policy question asks what happens to y if we intervene to change x. Accurate prediction does not answer the second question.

Features can predict well without being causes. Through confounding, a feature may simply track a hidden driver of the outcome. Through reverse causality, the outcome may cause the feature. Consider a model predicting student dropout. Rarely logging into the learning platform might be the strongest predictor, but forcing students to log in would not address the illness, money worries or disengagement behind both behaviours. A well-known example from medical prediction: a model learned that asthma patients with pneumonia had lower mortality, because those patients had received more intensive care. Acting on that pattern would have been harmful.

The ranking of features is also fragile. In regression, a coefficient depends on which other variables are included, which is the logic of omitted variable bias. Among correlated features, lasso may keep one and drop another almost arbitrarily, so 'importance' can shift between samples. Permutation importance and SHAP values describe how the model uses its inputs, not how the world works.

Intervening can break the model itself. A model trained on observational data assumes the relationships it saw will persist. Once a feature becomes a target, people may game it, as Goodhart's law warns, and the distribution shifts.

To learn what to change, we need causal designs: randomised experiments or A/B tests, or natural experiments analysed with instrumental variables, difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity, with credible assumptions. Predictive models are still valuable for targeting, such as identifying who needs support, for forecasting demand and for risk scoring. They can also suggest hypotheses worth testing.

In conclusion, accurate prediction tells us who is likely to experience an outcome, not why. Using feature importance as a policy guide without causal evidence risks ineffective or harmful interventions.
